idiom_name: interface AsyncQueue<T> over an array + resolvers, drained with for await...of
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds the contract, not a runtime: a bounded AsyncQueue<T> exposes push(item): Promise<void> (resolved when capacity frees) and an AsyncIterable<T>/AsyncGenerator<T> drain, consumers use for await...of, and the compiler enforces that producer items and consumer expectations agree. for-await requires targeting ES2018 or newer - downlevel iteration otherwise needs a Symbol.asyncIterator polyfill - and the bound and full-queue policy must be explicit in the type's options, because the type system cannot enforce capacity. Typed wrappers over node:stream (Transform/Readable with backpressure) or Web Streams are the library-backed alternatives; cross-thread work uses worker_threads MessagePort with structured-clone message types.
pitfalls: Types do not enforce the bound or the full-queue policy; an unbounded array behind a generic interface looks safe and is not.
AsyncGenerator<T> provides no backpressure by itself - a producer that never awaits fills memory.
Targeting ES2017 or lower breaks for-await: it needs the ES2018 lib and, on older runtimes, a Symbol.asyncIterator polyfill.
worker_threads messages are structured-cloned, so types that describe class instances crossing the boundary are a lie at runtime.

variants.name: Web Streams (ReadableStream<T> with pull backpressure)
variants.idiom_name: ReadableStream<T> with an underlying source whose pull() is called on demand
variants.implementation_notes: The Web Streams API reverses the hand-off: instead of the consumer asking a queue, the ReadableStream's underlying source exposes pull(controller), which the platform calls only when the consumer wants more data (internal queue below the high-water mark), so backpressure is built into the stream rather than added by the producer. Chunks are produced with controller.enqueue and terminated with controller.close(), a ReadableStream is async iterable so consumers can use for await...of, and pipeThrough/pipeTo compose stages (ReadableStream.from() adapts an async iterable into a stream). Typed as ReadableStream<T> it is the declarative, demand-driven alternative to a hand-written async queue, and it is available in Node 18+ and browsers.
pitfalls: pull() is demand-driven, so a producer that ignores the controller's queue (enqueueing eagerly in start()) loses the backpressure the API provides.
Iterating a stream locks it; a second consumer throws a TypeError until the lock is released, and exiting the loop cancels the stream unless preventCancel is used.
The high-water mark is a byte/chunk count, not a business-level capacity: derived bounds must be chosen deliberately.
